You have a multi-stage Dockerfile for a Go application, but the final image is still 800MB. Walk me through how you'd debug and reduce this — what specifically would you check in each stage?

docker history <image> or docker inspect to see the size contributed by each layer 
Checking whether the build stage artifacts are leaking into the final stage — e.g. are you actually doing COPY --from=build for only the compiled binary, or accidentally copying the whole build context/source/go module cache?
For Go specifically: confirming a static binary build (CGO_ENABLED=0) so you can go to scratch or distroless/static rather than needing glibc-based distroless.
Checking .dockerignore — is unnecessary build context (.git, node_modules-equivalents, test data) bloating layers?
Checking base image choice at the build stage too — using golang:1.x (huge) vs golang:1.x-alpine for the build stage doesn't matter for final size (it's discarded) but affects build time; the final stage base is what matters — scratch if no shell/debugging needed, distroless if you need minimal runtime (CA certs, timezone data).

records.rawDisplayText:
You're troubleshooting a container that can't reach another container on the same custom bridge network by container name, but it can reach it by IP. What's going on, and how do you fix it?

If it can reach via IP but not via name it is DNS resolve issue. I will see to what IP is the container name getting resolved or is it getting resolved at all. It's possible that either DNS server itself is down if it does not get resolved or maybe if it is getting resolved and take from there.

Mostly check things around DNS;

Thought for 7s

Rating: 5/10

What's good:

Correctly diagnosed the category of problem: DNS resolution, not routing/connectivity (since IP works, the network path itself is fine).

What's missing for a senior-level answer:

On a custom/user-defined bridge network, Docker runs an embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11 inside each container, and automatically registers containers by name for resolution. This is fundamentally different from the default bridge network, where automatic name-based DNS doesn't work at all (only legacy --link provided that). So the very first thing to verify is: are both containers actually attached to the same custom network? (docker network inspect <network> — a very common root cause is one container accidentally left on the default bridge or a different network).
Check /etc/resolv.conf inside the container to confirm nameserver 127.0.0.11 is present — if someone overrode DNS settings (e.g. --dns flag pointing elsewhere, or a base image with a baked-in resolv.conf), embedded DNS gets bypassed.
Check if the container was started with a custom --network-alias — the container is reachable by that alias but not by its container name, which is a very common trip-up.
Verify with docker exec <container> nslookup <other_container_name> or getent hosts to isolate whether it's DNS resolution itself failing or something after resolution (e.g. resolves to wrong/stale IP after a container restart, since IPs can change but old DNS cache lingered).
"DNS server itself is down" isn't really the likely failure mode here — Docker's embedded DNS is a lightweight internal daemon and rarely just "goes down"; misconfiguration or wrong-network attachment is far more common in practice, so I'd want you to lead with that rather than server health.

records.rawDisplayText:
Explain the difference between a Docker volume and a bind mount. Then describe a scenario in production where using a bind mount would actually be the wrong choice, and why.


Portability: bind mounts tie you to the exact host filesystem layout/path existing on that machine. In production, especially with orchestrators (Swarm, Kubernetes-adjacent thinking), containers get scheduled onto different nodes — a bind mount path that exists on Node A may not exist (or may have different content) on Node B. Volumes (especially named volumes backed by a volume driver/plugin) are the portable, orchestration-friendly choice.
Permissions/security: bind mounts expose host filesystem permissions and UID/GID mapping directly into the container — a classic scenario is mounting the Docker socket (/var/run/docker.sock) or a sensitive host path, which is a well-known privilege escalation risk (container escape vector). This is exactly the kind of "why is a bind mount wrong here" scenario expected at senior level.
Performance/isolation: on Docker Desktop (macOS/Windows), bind mounts go through a filesystem translation layer (e.g. osxfs/gRPC-FUSE) which is significantly slower than native volumes for I/O-heavy workloads — relevant for local dev-to-prod parity discussions.
Managed backups/drivers: volumes support volume drivers/plugins (e.g. for cloud block storage, NFS) enabling backup, replication, and multi-host storage — bind mounts have none of that; they're just a raw host path.
A concrete production scenario: mounting an app's config directly via bind mount from a specific host path in a multi-node Swarm/ECS cluster — works fine on a single dev machine, breaks the moment you scale to multiple hosts or redeploy on a different instance.
